loop: CRISP-DM loops: findings in the Evaluation phase can send the project back to Business Understanding for the next iteration.

phases.name: Business Understanding
phases.question: What problem is solved, for whom, and when is it a success?

steps.d: Spotting anxiety relies on the school counselor's observation: limited capacity, reactive and subjective.
Detect early, prioritize students, and recommend support with the reasons.
Predict an anxiety score from 0 to 10 and use it as a SMART criterion (where DM meets the DSS).
D1-D4 for the model (such as R² ≥ 0.60) and S1-S4 for the decision (such as ≥ 90% stable).

decisions: Data mining answers how high the anxiety is and which factors dominate; SMART answers who comes first and which support fits.
Five alternatives: sleep, exercise, study strategy, counseling, relaxation.
The system is a screening aid, not a clinical diagnosis.

rows: Use the prediction as a DSS criterion
Adapt the model to high-school students

phases.name: Data Understanding
phases.question: What data exists, how good is it, and which columns help?

steps.d: Kaggle (1M university-student rows, public) for pretraining; the high-school Google Form (confidential) for retraining.
Missing values, duplicates, plausible ranges; for the questionnaire also unknown answers and straight-lining.
Stress level and burnout relate most strongly to the anxiety score.
Outcome variables dropped (label leakage); columns with near-zero correlation that SMART does not need are not used.

decisions: mental_health_index, depression_score, dropout_risk and risk_level are outcomes, not causes: dropped to avoid leakage.
social_support, screen_time and internet_usage barely correlate: not used.
Age and report grade stay in although their linear correlation is small (r 0.01 and 0.05); the report grade is also a SMART criterion.
academic_year does not apply to high-school students.

phases.name: Data Preparation
phases.question: How does raw data become 11 model-ready features?

steps.d: Full 1M rows → student ages 14-25 only (692,545) → 80/20 split by age: 554,036 training rows, 138,509 test rows, random_state 42.
Gender to fixed codes (Female 0, Male 1, Other 2); questionnaire text answers → numbers.
Each item maps to 0-1, then to the Kaggle feature scale; the Psikologis items form the target.
Personal columns dropped once age is computed; blanks filled with the questionnaire medians.

decisions: Only rows in the student age band 14-25 are used. The Kaggle file spans 17-29, so ages 17-25 remain.

20,000 Kaggle test rows become the reference population (dataset.csv). No model is ever trained on them, so the report charts never use training rows. The real model's percentiles and referral cutoff come from the questionnaire respondents, which are also that model's training data.
No extra outlier removal: the data has no missing, duplicate or impossible values, and dropping extreme rows did not raise R².
Questionnaire items are merged into the 11 features before SMART; SMART never reads a raw answer.
Target items (P01-P05, plus P06-P07 on the revised form) are never features, so there is no label leakage.
SMART min-max bounds are saved with the model (Kaggle model: the 20,000 reference rows; real model: the questionnaire respondents), so a single student can be normalized.
Questionnaire data splits 80% development / 20% holdout, stratified by form version.

phases.name: Modeling
phases.question: Which algorithm predicts anxiety, and how does SMART decide?

steps.d: Regression with 300 trees: captures non-linear patterns, resists outliers, suits ordinal answers. Settings tuned by 5-fold cross-validation.
RF is on par with linear regression and gradient boosting, slightly above a single tree, and far above the mean baseline.
Min-max utility → priority score (mean) and a score per alternative (weight × utility).
Exact Shapley values per student, "what if" counterfactuals, permutation and PDP/ICE.

decisions: RF is kept although linear regression and gradient boosting are equally accurate on Kaggle (test R² 0.606-0.608): questionnaire data is ordinal, and RF lets the warm-start strategy (S3) be tested during retraining.
Hyperparameters come from a random search (25 settings, 5-fold CV on 50,000 training rows): depth 12, leaves of 50+ students, 75% of the features per split, 60% of the rows per tree.
Seven retraining strategies are compared with 5-fold CV × 2; the lowest MAE is deployed.

phases.name: Evaluation
phases.question: Is the model accurate, the decision stable and fair, and the business goal met?

steps.d: MAE, RMSE, R² on the test set, compared with 3 other algorithms and the mean baseline.
Weights moved ±10%/±20% per criterion and jittered 100 times.
MAE and recommendation mix by gender; Gini vs permutation; Shapley per student.
Black-box (from the specification) and white-box (from the code) tests, automated with pytest.

decisions: One domain-based weight set is used; its stability is checked by criterion S1.
The safety rule uses a percentile, because the RF pulls extreme predictions toward the middle.

phases.name: Deployment
phases.question: How do counselors use it, and how is it maintained?

steps.d: Bilingual (ID/EN), an App zone (4 pages) and a Report zone (8 chapters), hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud from a private repository.
Models are trained offline; the app only loads the .joblib and metadata and runs inference.
Upload new responses to measure the MAE; retrain as responses grow.
Nothing is stored, personal columns are dropped, aggregates under 5 people are hidden.

decisions: Streamlit was chosen (not Gradio) for multipage navigation, rich charts, caching and free hosting.
Library versions are pinned so the .joblib files load on the server.
pytest is run by hand before a release; there is no automated CI yet.
